place.en: the Atlantic coasts of Iberia and Africa
place.pt: the Atlantic coasts of Iberia and Africa

stages.name: Not attested
stages.desc: No Phoenician or Punic presence known, in texts or in the ground

stages.name: Known only from ancient reports
stages.desc: Described by Greek or Latin writers; no Punic finds yet

stages.name: Regular Punic trade
stages.desc: Phoenician and Punic goods and trading posts, few or no towns

stages.name: Phoenician/Punic settlement
stages.desc: Phoenician or Carthaginian towns, temples and harbours

states.name: Morocco
timeline: Lixus on the Loukkos estuary and the island trading post of Mogador
Mogador island is abandoned; Lixus, Tingis and the Kouass kilns carry on
Punic is written as far inland as Volubilis
Carthage falls; Polybius sails down this coast for Rome
King Bocchus II dies and leaves Mauretania to Rome
Augustus makes Juba II king of Mauretania; purple dye works follow on Mogador

states.name: W. Sahara
timeline: Desert coast facing the Canaries; no Phoenician finds
Hanno's Periplus describes a southward voyage; his island of Cerne is often placed at Herne island, off Dakhla
A Greek sailing guide says Phoenicians trade at Cerne with Africans of the mainland

states.name: Spain
timeline: Gadir, Malaka, Sexi and Abdera on the southern coast, Ebusus on Ibiza; the Canary Islands share Spain's colour here, but no settlement there is proven
Carthage's second treaty with Rome bars Roman ships beyond Mastia, near later Cartagena
Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir and begins a Carthaginian conquest of the south
Hasdrubal founds Qart Hadasht, 'New Carthage', at Cartagena
Gadir goes over to Rome; Carthage's rule in Spain ends, but Punic towns keep their language, gods and coins
Sailors at the mouth of the Guadalquivir tell Sertorius of two Atlantic islands

states.name: Portugal
timeline: Phoenician traders at Abul on the Sado, at Tavira, Santa Olaia and Lisbon; Madeira and the Azores, shown in Portugal's colour, are unknown
Gaditan traders keep working the coast after the old Phoenician posts decline
Roman armies under Decimus Junius Brutus march north past the Tagus to the Douro

states.name: Mauritania
timeline: Saharan and Sahelian coast beyond any known Phoenician sailing
Hanno's account of a great river full of crocodiles and hippopotami may describe the Senegal

events.title: Temple at Gadir
events.text: Gadir's temple of Melqart, the Phoenician Hercules, stands at the edge of the known world and draws sailors from across the Mediterranean.

events.title: Lixus
events.text: On a hill above the Loukkos, Lixus is one of the oldest Phoenician towns on Africa's Atlantic coast.

events.title: Mogador trading post
events.text: Phoenician ships call at a small island off Essaouira, trading wine and fine pottery for ivory and skins.

events.title: Abul
events.text: A fortified Phoenician trading house stands on the Sado estuary in southern Portugal.

events.title: Malaka
events.text: Malaka, today's Málaga, is one of a string of Phoenician towns on Spain's southern coast.

events.title: Silver of Huelva
events.text: Phoenician demand for silver from the Tartessian mines makes Huelva one of the richest ports of the west.

events.title: Mogador abandoned
events.text: The island post off Essaouira falls silent; no one will work there again for nearly five centuries.

events.title: Hanno sails
events.text: The Carthaginian Hanno takes sixty ships through the Strait to found colonies on the African coast, as his Periplus tells it.

events.title: Thymiaterion
events.text: Hanno's first foundation, Thymiaterion, is often placed near Mehdia, at the mouth of the Sebou.

events.title: Cerne
events.text: Hanno settles colonists on a small island he calls Cerne, perhaps Herne island in the bay of Dakhla.

events.title: River of crocodiles
events.text: Hanno describes a wide river full of crocodiles and hippopotami, perhaps the Senegal.

events.title: Himilco sails north
events.text: Another Carthaginian, Himilco, sails north along Iberia and reports calm seas, shallows, weed and sea monsters.

events.title: Kouass kilns
events.text: Potters at Kouass, near Asilah, make Punic amphorae for the salted fish of the Strait.

events.title: Gadir's fish
events.text: Salted fish and fish sauce from Gadir are shipped as far as Corinth and Athens.

events.title: Buenavista claim
events.text: Excavators date a site at Buenavista, on Lanzarote, to Phoenician and Punic times; most specialists doubt such early dates.

events.title: Trade at Cerne
events.text: A Greek sailing guide says Phoenician merchants unload perfume, pottery and Egyptian stone at Cerne, for skins and ivory.

events.title: Treaty with Rome
events.text: Carthage's second treaty with Rome forbids Roman ships to trade or found towns beyond Mastia in Spain.

events.title: Pytheas passes Gades
events.text: The Greek Pytheas of Massalia slips past Carthage's Strait on his voyage to the far north.

events.title: The Corvo hoard?
events.text: Carthaginian and Cyrenaic coins of about this date were reported found on Corvo in 1749; the coins are lost and the find unverified.

events.title: The forbidden island
events.text: A Greek collection of marvels tells of a fertile island days beyond the Strait; Carthage forbade sailing there on pain of death.

events.title: Punic at Volubilis
events.text: Punic inscriptions show that Carthage's language and gods reached the Moroccan interior.

events.title: Hamilcar lands
events.text: After losing Sicily, Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir to win a new empire in Spain.

events.title: New Carthage
events.text: Hasdrubal founds Qart Hadasht on a fine harbour; the Romans will call it Carthago Nova.

events.title: Siege of Saguntum
events.text: Hannibal takes Saguntum, Rome's ally, and the Second Punic War begins.

events.title: Scipio takes New Carthage
events.text: Publius Cornelius Scipio storms Carthage's capital in Spain in a single day.

events.title: Battle of Ilipa
events.text: Scipio destroys Carthage's last great army in Spain, near Seville.

events.title: Gadir turns to Rome
events.text: Gadir shuts its gates to the Carthaginian fleet and makes a treaty with Rome.

events.title: Two Spains
events.text: Rome divides its Spanish conquests into two provinces, Nearer and Further Spain.

events.title: Polybius explores
events.text: As Carthage is destroyed, the historian Polybius sails down Morocco's Atlantic coast with a Roman fleet.

events.title: Brutus at the Douro
events.text: Decimus Junius Brutus leads a Roman army across the Douro into the far north-west.

events.title: Eudoxus sails
events.text: Eudoxus of Cyzicus sails from Gades to reach India around Africa, and is never heard of again.

events.title: Isles of the Blest
events.text: Near the mouth of the Guadalquivir, sailors tell the Roman rebel Sertorius of two blessed islands far out in the ocean.

events.title: Caesar at Gades
events.text: The young quaestor Julius Caesar visits the temple of Hercules at Gades.

events.title: Diodorus's island
events.text: Diodorus of Sicily writes of a huge, well-watered island far out in the ocean, which Carthage kept as its secret refuge.

events.title: Bocchus II dies
events.text: Mauretania's last king of the old line dies and leaves his kingdom to Rome.

events.title: Juba II crowned
events.text: Augustus makes Juba II, a scholar raised in Rome, king of Mauretania.

events.title: The Fortunate Isles
events.text: Juba's ships go on to explore the Fortunate Isles, today's Canaries, and he describes them island by island.

events.title: Purple of Mogador
events.text: Juba's workers dye cloth with murex purple on Mogador and on the Purple Islands that Pliny mentions.

events.title: Lobos workshop
events.text: On tiny Lobos, off Fuerteventura, a Roman-era purple dye camp worked from about the mid-first century BC.

events.title: El Bebedero
events.text: At El Bebedero, on Lanzarote, Roman amphora sherds and metal appear in layers dated from about this time.

eras: The Voyages of Hanno and Himilco
chartNote: Share of the area of five present-day countries (Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Western Sahara and Mauritania), coloured by the strongest evidence for Phoenician or Punic presence anywhere in each. A simplification: borders are today's, one coastal town colours a whole country, and the Atlantic islands take their country's colour although no Phoenician or Punic settlement on them is proven.
